In the Hebrew Bible, it occurs four times, all within Judges 7:24, so its meaning is tied to identifying that location. The available renderings preserve it as a name instead of translating it into a broader concept. Without the surrounding verse text, no further contextual meaning should be added.

e.t: This Hebrew noun means “corn,” referring to the crop or food produce that can be gathered, stored, given, or traded. It appears 14 times in the Old Testament corpus, including passages describing Joseph’s provisions and the buying and selling of produce. The word therefore names a tangible agricultural product rather than an action or quality. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its ordinary sense remains corn as harvested produce.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a “bath,” a measured quantity used for liquids. It functions as a noun naming a unit of capacity rather than an action or description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 13 times across eight verses, especially in passages describing vessels, liquid measures, offerings, and commerce. Its use in 1 Kings, 2 Chronicles, Isaiah, and Ezekiel consistently centers on measuring liquid quantities. The surrounding verse determines what liquid is being measured, but the word itself identifies the measure.

This Hebrew verb means “shave”—to remove hair by cutting it away. It is used for shaving the head, beard, or body, and can describe either the act itself or the resulting removal of hair. The word appears 23 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Ezekiel. Its use in instructions about cleansing and in accounts involving hair shows a straightforward physical action rather than a special title or abstract idea. The precise significance of shaving in any particular passage depends on the surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “faint,” describing a weakened or failing condition. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and each occurrence is rendered “faint.” The word appears in Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Lamentations, showing that it can describe a condition recognized in different prophetic and lament settings. Its central idea remains the same: being faint rather than strong or vigorous. The surrounding verse supplies the specific reason or situation connected with that condition.

In Hebrew, דָּלַל means “low.” It expresses a condition rather than identifying a person, place, or object. The word occurs nine times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its precise force depends on the sentence in which it appears. It can function predicatively, describing the condition of what is being discussed. In the SEE relationships, it appears in descriptions where a subject is characterized by this condition.

This Hebrew word expresses a person’s inward turning “for” something—the object toward which longing or strong wanting is directed. It can describe desire involving people, possessions, food, or water, so its force may be honorable or improper depending on what is sought. In the Old Testament, it occurs 28 times across 25 verses, including passages connected with coveting and longing. Its precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence and what the person is turning toward.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “males,” referring to male human persons. It functions as a noun identifying the male members of a group. In its four Old Testament occurrences, it is used in instructions concerning Israel’s appointed appearances before God and in an account involving people defeated in conflict. Thus, its basic meaning remains focused on male persons rather than on a broader group or an abstract quality.

This Hebrew word refers to “armour,” the protective equipment associated with warfare. It appears twice in the Old Testament, both times in First Kings. As a noun, it identifies a tangible object rather than an action, quality, or person. Its precise role in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and sentence, but its ordinary sense points to protective battle equipment. The word is therefore best understood as a term for armour or war gear within the Hebrew Bible.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to a thistle, a prickly plant. It functions as a plant term in the Old Testament and is used for vegetation that can grow in neglected or unproductive places. It also appears in comparisons, where a thistle represents something weak, unsuitable, or easily damaged when set against something stronger. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with the dominant rendering “thistle.” Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

Hul is a personal name, rendered as “Hul.” It identifies an individual in the Hebrew Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs twice, once in Genesis 10:23 and once in 1 Chronicles 1:17. Because no fuller lexical definition is provided, its ordinary use is best understood as a proper name whose significance comes from the genealogy or family listing where it appears.

This Hebrew word means “sinners,” referring to people characterized by sin or wrongdoing. It functions as a noun, naming such people rather than describing a single sinful act. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 19 times. Its ordinary sense identifies a person by sinful conduct, while the surrounding verse determines the particular warning, contrast, or statement being made about those people.

Helon is a personal name, referring to a man identified in Israel’s wilderness-era community. It is rendered “Helon” and appears five times in the Hebrew Old Testament, all in Numbers. Because no short definition or descriptive meaning is provided, the word functions primarily as a proper name rather than as a general term describing an object, action, or quality. Its precise significance in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the name itself identifies the same biblical figure wherever it occurs.

The word refers to a “hypocrite”—a person identified by that description. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 13 times, so it is an established term rather than a one-time expression. Its recorded uses are concentrated especially in Job, with additional occurrences in Psalms, Proverbs, and Isaiah. The word’s precise force in any particular sentence depends on the surrounding verse, but its central lexical sense remains “hypocrite.”

This Hebrew noun means “artificer,” referring to a person identified by skilled making or workmanship. It occurs twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, once in Genesis 4:22 and once in 1 Kings 7:14. In ordinary sentences, it identifies the person associated with creating or working skillfully. The surrounding verse determines the particular work or setting intended, but the word itself points to the maker rather than to the object produced.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to cleansing or purification—the state or process of being made clean. It is used especially in passages describing ceremonial purification after childbirth, skin conditions, or contact with death. Thus, it can describe the period or condition connected with becoming clean before returning to ordinary life or worship. The word occurs 15 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, with many uses in Leviticus and further occurrences in Nehemiah, Chronicles, and Ezekiel.

This Hebrew word expresses “defer” or “slack.” It describes an action that is not carried out promptly, whether referring to a person’s response, an obligation, or an awaited act. Its meaning centers on postponement or a lack of timely action, while the surrounding sentence determines the precise application. It occurs 17 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Habakkuk. Scripture uses it in both human actions and statements about God’s purposes or appointed timing.

This Hebrew word is the personal name “Job.” It refers to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Genesis 46:13. The name itself identifies the person; its precise significance in that passage must come from the surrounding verse and larger biblical context, not from the name alone.

Each occurrence belongs to genealogical material, where the name is connected with birth or descent. The available information supports understanding Jalam as the individual’s identifying name; it does not provide a separate lexical definition or explain the name’s etymology.

It functions as a designation for those associated with Abiezer rather than as a general description or action. The word occurs six times, all in Judges, appearing in three verses from Judges 6 through Judges 8. Its use identifies the group as a participant or associated party in the surrounding account, while the exact role in any particular verse depends on that verse’s context.

e.t: The word means “formed”: it describes the act of bringing something into a made condition. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it is used broadly for things that are formed, including wording connected with God’s work and with a potter’s work. Its central idea is deliberate formation rather than mere existence. The word occurs 63 times in 56 verses, so the precise object and force are supplied by each sentence’s context.

This word is a personal name, rendered “Jerusha” or “Jerushah.” It identifies the same woman in two Old Testament occurrences, appearing once in 2 Kings and once in 2 Chronicles. The two English spellings represent a difference in rendering, not two separate names or meanings. As a name, its precise significance is not defined by the available lexical information; its main function is to identify a person in the biblical record.

Jeshishai is a Hebrew personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing a general idea or action. Its meaning is not defined by an available lexical gloss; the surviving English rendering presents the name as “Jeshishai.” This name occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 5:14. Without the surrounding verse text, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or the role he has in that passage.

This Hebrew word refers to Chisloth, a place name rather than a description of an action, quality, or object. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, both occurrences being in Joshua 19:12. The same verse also associates the name with Tabor, showing that it functions as a geographic designation within a boundary description. Its precise location and role are best understood from the surrounding passage, but the word itself identifies the place called Chisloth.

This Hebrew word means “provision,” naming something supplied for a need. It functions as a noun rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in 2 Kings 6:23. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense is the provision itself—the thing made available or supplied. Its core idea remains an action around something rather than a person, object, or abstract quality.

e.t: Lot is a personal name, referring to the man who appears in the family line of Terah and traveled with Abram. As a name, it identifies a particular person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 33 times, chiefly in Genesis. The name also appears in passages describing God’s dealings with Lot and the land connected with his descendants.

This Hebrew word means “out.” It functions as a brief directional or positional expression, marking something as out rather than describing an object, person, or action by itself. The word appears once in the Hebrew Bible corpus, in Proverbs 25:19. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic contribution is the idea expressed by “out.”

Mehida is a personal name, rendered “Mehida,” rather than a word that describes an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs two times, appearing once in Ezra 2:52 and once in Nehemiah 7:54. No separate lexical definition is provided, so it is best understood here as the name itself; any specific significance depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word means “settings,” functioning as a noun for designated places where something is set in place. It occurs three times in the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, all in Exodus, in descriptions involving the arrangement of precious stones. Its basic sense is therefore a setting or fitted position, rather than the stone itself. The surrounding passage is needed to explain its specific use in each occurrence.

The Hebrew word refers to “eyes.” It functions as a noun naming the organs of sight. This form occurs once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Song 5:12, so its ordinary lexical range cannot be established from repeated uses across different passages. In that occurrence, it serves as the object in two relationships involving the eyes. The surrounding verse supplies the details of those relationships; the basic meaning itself is simply “eyes.”

This Hebrew word means “these,” pointing to specific people or things already identified in the sentence or surrounding discussion. It functions as a demonstrative pronoun, directing attention to particular subjects rather than speaking of them generally. The word appears five times in the Hebrew text, all in Daniel, where it helps identify people or things under discussion. Its exact reference in each passage comes from the surrounding wording.

This Hebrew word describes someone or something as “mighty”—strong, powerful, or capable of prevailing. It is used six times in the Old Testament, appearing in Genesis, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its repeated rendering as “mighty” points to a consistent central idea of strength and power rather than a narrow or specialized meaning. The surrounding verse determines whether the word describes a person, God, or another source of strength, but its basic sense remains mightiness or powerful ability.

e.t: This Hebrew noun refers to “shewbread,” a designated bread used in Israel’s worship. It names a particular kind of bread, rather than an action, person, or quality. The term occurs nine times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, with its uses concentrated in descriptions connected with the tabernacle and temple service. Its exact force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains the worship-associated bread identified as shewbread.

This Hebrew noun refers to “deep,” describing a great distance below the surface or a deep place. It is used for the deep associated with waters and for situations in which someone is overwhelmed or surrounded by them. The word occurs 11 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including several uses in the Psalms and accounts of God’s deliverance through the sea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: Merodach is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. It identifies a particular named figure or entity in the Hebrew text, so its role is to name rather than to describe an action, quality, or object. In the Hebrew Bible corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 50:2, and is rendered “Merodach.” Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself functions as a name, not as a broad vocabulary term.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to “friends”—people connected to someone through personal association. It is used for those regarded as part of a person’s social circle, whether in ordinary relationships or in speech about loyalty and personal standing. The word occurs seven times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing a focused meaning rather than a broad description of every kind of relationship. Its precise force in any passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation.

This Hebrew word refers to hatred—a strong feeling of hostility or opposition toward someone. It appears twice in the Hebrew Old Testament, both times in Hosea 9:7–8. In these passages, the word describes an attitude directed against another person, so it points to active enmity rather than simple dislike. Its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central meaning is hatred or hostile opposition.

This Hebrew word means “banquet.” It is a noun naming a meal occasion, rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, at Daniel 5:10. Because it has a single recorded occurrence, “banquet” is the clearest ordinary meaning for understanding the word at the lexical level. The surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain its particular significance there.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “serpent,” referring to the snake-like creature named in the Old Testament. It is used for serpents in several settings, including Genesis, the wilderness account in Numbers, and later prophetic writings. The word occurs 31 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, and its surrounding scriptural associations can include danger, death, speech, judgment, and destruction. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Hebrew word functions as a term rendered “brought,” describing an action in which something is brought. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, at Proverbs 8:30. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the word’s precise role in that sentence cannot be explained further without adding details not present in the passage. Its basic contribution is the idea of bringing, as expressed by its recorded rendering.

“Neah” is a Hebrew place name, referring to a named location rather than describing an action, quality, or person. It appears once in the Hebrew Old Testament, in Joshua 19:13. Because it functions as a proper name, its meaning is primarily the identification of that location, not a broader concept or activity. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain its specific role in that passage.

This Hebrew noun refers to a “whirlwind,” a forceful rotating storm. It names a natural storm that can arrive suddenly and bring overwhelming power. In the Old Testament, the word occurs 16 times, appearing in descriptions of storms and in comparisons that portray sudden, fearsome judgment or distress. Its use presents the storm as an active, powerful force rather than merely ordinary weather.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of being “covered,” describing something placed beneath or enclosed by another thing. It functions as a verbal expression rather than naming an object. The word appears 24 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, including descriptions associated with the sanctuary and other physical settings. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being covered and the surrounding sentence.

The word occurs 59 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, showing that it commonly names natural rock formations rather than expressing an abstract idea. Its precise force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

e.t: This Hebrew word means “lead,” referring to the metal. It functions as a noun, naming a material rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs nine times, including passages in Exodus, Numbers, Job, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah. Its uses include descriptions of material involved in giving, speech, and comparison. The surrounding verse determines the particular image or purpose, but the word itself consistently identifies lead as the central object or material.

This Hebrew word expresses the idea of “forsaking.” It refers to the act of turning away or leaving something behind, with its precise force determined by the surrounding sentence. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs once, in Isaiah 6:12. The available rendering presents it as “forsaking,” giving the clearest supported sense for this rare word. Its use there is connected with the Lord and what is left behind, but the verse text is needed to explain the full context.

“Troubles” is the clearest meaning of this Hebrew word. It names a troubling condition or set of circumstances, functioning as a descriptive term rather than a personal name or place-name. In the Hebrew Old Testament corpus, it occurs only once, at Daniel 4:9. Since the verse text and surrounding passage are not available here, the word’s precise use in that verse cannot be described beyond this central sense.

Anim is a Hebrew proper name preserved in English as “Anim.” It functions as a specific name rather than a descriptive word with a broader stated meaning. This Hebrew word occurs once, in Joshua 15:50, and both recorded English renderings preserve the name as “Anim.” The available information identifies the name and its occurrence, but does not provide an additional lexical definition or explain the surrounding verse. Its precise significance in Joshua 15:50 therefore belongs to the verse’s context.

This Hebrew noun means “beds,” referring to prepared places where plants grow. It occurs four times in the Old Testament Hebrew corpus, appearing in Song of Solomon and Ezekiel. Its ordinary sense is a defined area set apart for growth, whether in a garden or cultivated land. The surrounding passage determines the precise picture in each occurrence, but the word itself points to beds as places prepared for vegetation.

This Hebrew word means “Ancient” and functions as a descriptive word for someone presented as ancient. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs three times, all in Daniel 7. Its uses are associated with Daniel 7:9, 7:13, and 7:22, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each passage’s particular force. As a lexical word, it describes ancient identity or status rather than naming an action.

The word therefore has a concrete, ordinary meaning rather than expressing an action, quality, or abstract idea.

e.t: This Hebrew word refers to what or who has escaped, functioning as a noun-like expression for the escaped portion or people remaining after danger or destruction. Its approved rendering is “escaped.” It occurs 28 times in the Hebrew Old Testament, from Genesis through Obadiah, showing that it can describe a remaining group or portion across different situations. The precise emphasis in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

This Hebrew word means “do.” It functions as an action word, describing what someone carries out or brings about in a sentence. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it occurs 56 times, so it is a recurring way to express action rather than a rare or specialized idea. Its SEE relationships also show it serving as the predicate—the part of a sentence that states what is done or happens. The surrounding words determine who performs the action and what is being done.

This Hebrew noun refers to “asps,” a kind of snake. It names the creature itself rather than describing an action or quality. The word occurs six times in the Hebrew Old Testament, appearing in passages from Deuteronomy, Job, Psalms, and Isaiah. Its uses consistently identify a dangerous snake, while the surrounding verse supplies the particular image or point being made.
